analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling in Georges Bank and marine sanctuaries.
analysis.headline: The Georges Bank Preservation Act never left committee: it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee on February 2, 2009 and died there when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, without a hearing, a vote, or a single action after its subcommittee referrals.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would permanently prohibit the federal government from issuing any lease or authorization for oil or gas exploration, development, or production in Georges Bank off New England, one of the nation's most important fishing grounds, and in any marine national monument or national marine sanctuary. It also directs the Commerce Department to map the exact boundaries of Georges Bank after public notice and comment. The stated aim is to protect the fishing grounds and protected ocean areas from drilling. The bill never advanced past referral to committee and subcommittee, and it received no votes before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Commercial fishermen and the coastal communities of New England whose livelihoods depend on Georges Bank, one of the largest and historically most important fishing grounds in the United States, would gain permanent legal protection from drilling that could disturb the grounds and risk spills. Marine sanctuaries and monuments nationwide would get the same shield. The public broadly would keep these areas off limits to drilling rather than relying on temporary moratoria that Congress can lift.
analysis.who_benefits_short: New England fishing communities and coastal areas

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any federal lease or authorization for oil or gas exploration, development, or production in Georges Bank, which the bill describes as one of the largest and historically important fishing grounds of the United States.
Extends the same drilling prohibition to every marine national monument and national marine sanctuary, protecting protected ocean areas nationwide rather than just Georges Bank.
Requires the Commerce Secretary to define the specific coordinates of Georges Bank after public notice and an opportunity for comment, so the protected area has legally clear boundaries.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to potential drilling areas in Georges Bank and in marine sanctuaries and monuments. The federal Treasury would forgo any lease revenue from those areas, and the nation would forgo some domestic oil and gas production. New England fishing fleets would bear the risk that drilling, if it ever occurred, could harm fish stocks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies seeking offshore leases

drawbacks.text: The bill would take potential oil and gas resources permanently off the table, reducing domestic energy production and the federal lease revenue those resources could generate.

The prohibition reaches beyond Georges Bank to every marine monument and sanctuary in the country, a broader ban than a New England-only measure, which energy producers would argue is wider than the spill risk justifies.
A statutory ban is a blunt tool: a permanent prohibition removes the ability to weigh drilling against fisheries on a case-by-case basis as technology and conditions change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is permanent, targeted protection for a fishery and a set of protected ocean areas against an industrial activity with known spill and disturbance risks; the cost is forgone energy production and lease revenue of uncertain size. Because existing protections for these waters were temporary and politically reversible, making the ban permanent had real value for the fishing industry, but the breadth of the nationwide monument and sanctuary ban drew reasonable objection, and the bill received no committee action at all, so no trade-off was ever formally weighed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and two of its subcommittees on February 2 and 4, 2009, and no further action was ever taken; it sat in committee until the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Markey of Massachusetts introduced the Georges Bank Preservation Act on February 2, 2009 with 13 cosponsors, all of them Democratic members from New England and New York.

The House referred the bill to the Committee on Natural Resources, which referred it to the Subcommittee on Insular Affairs, Oceans and Wildlife and the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources on February 4, 2009.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place; the full action history ends with the two subcommittee referrals.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and all bills not enacted by then expire, so the bill died in committee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests kept open the possibility of future access to Georges Bank and protected marine areas, and nothing changed for anyone: the moratorium framework in place before the bill remained as it was. Fishing communities received no permanent statutory protection and remain dependent on annually renewing or administratively reversible restrictions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas interests; nothing changed

for.name: Rep. Ed Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 2, 2009 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 14 of 253 House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors, all from New England and New York
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors of the bill at introduction.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Nick Rahall (D-WV)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no report in two years.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Had an interest in keeping Georges Bank and marine sanctuaries available for potential leasing; the record does not show industry action on this specific bill, which never became active legislation.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists; its sponsor and all 14 cosponsors were Democrats from New England and New York, and the committee that never acted was controlled by Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from any federal lease or authorization to explore for or produce oil and gas in Georges Bank, marine monuments, and sanctuaries, removing potential offshore acreage and future lease revenue. Drilling in a major fishing ground creates spill and disturbance risks that fall on the fishing economy and coastal communities, so the industry's interest in this bill ran against the communities it would operate beside.

Georges Bank is one of the largest and most historically important fishing grounds in the United States, and a permanent statutory drilling ban would protect the fishery and the fishing economy from spill and disruption risk. Because the bill never became law, this gain never arrived.

The government would lose the ability to offer leases in these areas and the associated bonus bids and royalties, in exchange for protecting resource areas with high commercial and environmental value.
